claims.text: Solomon receives wisdom as a divine gift, yet Kings and Sirach preserve a later collapse of covenant loyalty.
The dedication treats the Temple as a real place of name, glory, prayer, and covenant memory while denying that heaven can contain God.
The reign’s abundance is paired canonically with systems of provision and a later complaint about a grievous yoke.
The canon associates Solomon with sayings, songs, wisdom, editorial collections, and royal voices through several distinct literary forms.
Bathsheba bears a son named Solomon; the LORD loves him and sends the name Jedidiah through Nathan.

David identifies the future Temple site, gathers foreign workers and materials, tells Solomon that the promised son of rest will build, and commands Israel’s leaders to help.

David names Solomon as the chosen builder and calls him to know God, serve wholeheartedly, and seek God.
David gives Solomon plans, weights, divisions, and a pattern received by the Spirit, then points to workers and leaders.
David gives from royal and personal treasure and invites leaders to consecrate themselves by giving.
David gives from royal and personal treasure and invites leaders to consecrate themselves by giving.
The assembly worships, offers sacrifices, and makes Solomon king a second time; Solomon sits on the LORD’s throne.
Adonijah exalts himself, gathers supporters, sacrifices, and excludes Solomon while Nathan and Bathsheba alert David.

David orders Solomon placed on the royal mule and anointed; the city rejoices while Adonijah’s gathering dissolves.

Adonijah is executed after requesting Abishag, Abiathar is removed, Joab is killed, Benaiah is elevated, and Shimei dies after breaking an oath.

Officials, priests, secretaries, commanders, household managers, and twelve district governors are named.
